abstract: L-phenylalanine (Phe), an aromatic amino acid known to induce plant pathogen resistance at concentrations >4 mM, also functions as a broad-spectrum plant growth biostimulator in the total absence of biotic stress. To evaluate its biostimulatory potential, drench and foliar spray applications of Phe (1-16 mM) were tested on dicotyledonous (cucumber, tomato, lettuce) and monocotyledonous (wheat) crops grown under commercial-like net-house conditions with full NPK fertigation (150 mg/ L N). Weekly applications significantly enhanced vegetative growth across all species, increasing plant height by [≥]22-26%, node numbers by [≥]23-40%, and leaf/leaflet area by [≥]36-48% in cucumber and tomato, as well as expanding leaf area in lettuce. In reproductive stages, Phe treatments increased flower initiation, set fruits ([≥]23-27%), total fruit number ([≥]31%), and fruit yield per plant ([≥]30-36%) in cucumber and tomato. In wheat, Phe increased tiller formation, total spike counts by [≥]36%, and fresh/dry plant biomass. Growth enhancement required a strict concentration threshold of [≥]4 mM; lower concentrations (1-2 mM) were inconsistent, and applying 2 mM twice weekly failed to replicate the significant gains of a single 4 mM weekly treatment. Because background fertigation provided a continuous and ample nitrogen supply, periodic trace applications of Phe contributed negligible amounts of nutritional N or C. This supports the conclusion that Phe acts through concentration-dependent physiological and metabolic biostimulation rather than nutrient supplementation.
